title: Benign Conditions of the Vagina and Vulva
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)

overview.intro: This chapter covers two groups of benign lower genital tract conditions: the Bartholin duct cyst and abscess, and pelvic organ prolapse of the vaginal walls (cystocele, urethrocele, and rectocele). Both are explained from normal anatomy. The Bartholin gland keeps secreting into a blocked duct, so the duct swells. The pelvic organs are held up by a muscular floor and a connective tissue suspension, so damage to either lets an organ push the vaginal wall ahead of it. Board questions turn on location (posterolateral vestibule, anterior or posterior wall, upper or lower anterior wall) and on the symptom each location produces.

connections.how: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis can infect a Bartholin duct, although most abscesses are polymicrobial.
Stress incontinence from a hypermobile urethra and residual urine from a cystocele follow from how abdominal pressure is shared between bladder and urethra.
Abnormal collagen (Ehlers-Danlos) or fibrillin (Marfan) weakens the pelvic suspension and raises prolapse risk.
A rectocele creates a pocket in front of the rectum that traps stool during straining, causing obstructed defecation.
Loss of estrogen thins the vaginal epithelium and reduces collagen in the supporting tissues.

terms.def: Greater vestibular gland, a paired mucus-secreting gland in the superficial perineal pouch whose duct opens into the posterolateral vestibule.
The space between the labia minora into which the urethra, vagina, and vestibular gland ducts open.
Dilation of a blocked Bartholin duct by retained mucus.
A collection of pus that forms when a blocked duct or gland becomes infected.
Descent of a pelvic organ, with the vaginal wall or apex ahead of it, because its support has failed.
The muscular pelvic floor (pubococcygeus, puborectalis, iliococcygeus) that keeps the urogenital hiatus closed.
The midline gap in the levator ani through which the urethra and vagina pass.
The fibromuscular connective tissue that suspends the pelvic organs and attaches the vagina to the pelvic side walls.
Herniation of the bladder into the upper anterior vaginal wall.
Herniation of the urethra into the distal anterior vaginal wall.
Herniation of the rectum into the posterior vaginal wall through a weak rectovaginal septum.
Involuntary leakage of urine when abdominal pressure rises suddenly, as with coughing, laughing, or lifting.

blocks.text: The Bartholin glands, or greater vestibular glands, are paired pea-sized glands lying in the superficial perineal pouch at the posterior ends of the bulbs of the vestibule. Each drains through a duct about 2 cm long that opens into the vestibule lateral to the hymen, at about the 4 and 8 o'clock positions of the vaginal opening. The glands secrete mucus that lubricates the vestibule, especially during sexual arousal. They develop from the urogenital sinus, as do their male homologs, the bulbourethral (Cowper) glands.

A Bartholin duct cyst forms when the duct opening is blocked, most often by inflammation, edema, trauma, or thick mucus. The gland keeps secreting, and because the fluid cannot escape, the duct dilates behind the obstruction. The result is a usually unilateral, round, often painless mass in the posterolateral vestibule, commonly 1 to 3 cm across. Small cysts may cause no symptoms, while larger ones cause pressure, discomfort with sitting or walking, and dyspareunia.

blocks.title: From blocked duct to abscess
steps: Duct opening blocked by inflammation, edema, or mucus
Duct dilates into a cyst in the posterolateral vestibule
Neutrophils and pus raise pressure in a closed space
blocks.caption: A cyst is retained secretion; an abscess is the same closed space after infection.

blocks.text: An abscess forms when the retained secretion becomes infected, either in a pre-existing cyst or in the gland itself. Most abscesses are polymicrobial, with skin, vaginal, and bowel flora such as Escherichia coli and anaerobes; Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are found less often. Pus accumulates under pressure in a closed space, so the swelling becomes red, hot, fluctuant, and very tender, and it develops quickly over 2 to 4 days. Pain is often severe enough to prevent sitting or walking, and surrounding cellulitis or fever may accompany it.

Age is an important clue. These lesions occur mainly in reproductive-age women, when the glands are active. The glands shrink after menopause, so a new Bartholin mass in an older woman is less likely to be a simple cyst, and Bartholin gland carcinoma, though rare, must be excluded by biopsy. Location also separates the Bartholin cyst from look-alikes: a Skene (paraurethral) duct cyst sits beside the urethral opening, and an epidermal inclusion cyst usually lies in the labia.

blocks.title: Bartholin cyst and Bartholin abscess
rows: Infection of the retained secretion or gland
Severe; sitting and walking are painful
Red, hot, tender, fluctuant mass, sometimes cellulitis
Usually polymicrobial; occasionally gonococcal or chlamydial
blocks.caption: Both sit in the posterolateral vestibule; infection and pressure account for every difference.

blocks.predict: Would a Bartholin cyst be expected to arise in a 70-year-old woman as often as in a 25-year-old?
blocks.explain: No. The gland atrophies after menopause and secretes little, so obstruction rarely produces a cyst; a new mass at that age raises concern for carcinoma.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on age and the differential.

blocks.text: The pelvic organs are supported by two systems that work together. The levator ani muscles form a muscular floor with constant resting tone that keeps the urogenital hiatus nearly closed and holds the pelvic organs on a shelf. Above this floor, the endopelvic fascia and its thickenings suspend the organs: the cardinal and uterosacral ligaments hold the cervix and upper vagina, the pubocervical fascia supports the anterior vaginal wall and bladder, and the rectovaginal septum supports the posterior wall. Distally the vagina fuses with the perineal body and perineal membrane.

blocks.title: Levels of vaginal support
rows: Uterine or vaginal vault prolapse, enterocele
Pubocervical fascia and rectovaginal septum attached to the pelvic side walls
Perineal body, perineal membrane, levator ani
Urethrocele and urethral hypermobility, low rectocele, perineal descent
blocks.caption: The three-level description of vaginal support (DeLancey) predicts which defect produces which prolapse.

blocks.text: While the levator ani is intact and the hiatus is closed, the connective tissue carries little load. When the muscle is torn or denervated, the hiatus widens and the organs rest on the fascia and ligaments alone. Connective tissue under constant load slowly stretches and does not recover, so the vaginal walls descend and the organ behind each wall follows it. This explains why prolapse often appears years after the injury that began it.

blocks.title: How vaginal childbirth leads to prolapse
steps: Fetal head distends the levator ani and pelvic floor
Muscle tears or avulses from the pubic bone
Stretch injures pudendal and levator nerves
Weak floor lets the urogenital hiatus widen
Fascia and ligaments bear the load alone
Connective tissue stretches and the vaginal walls descend
blocks.caption: The floor fails first; the suspension then fails gradually under constant load.

blocks.text: Vaginal childbirth is the strongest risk factor, and risk rises with the number of vaginal deliveries, a large baby, and a long second stage of labor. Aging adds loss of muscle mass and weaker collagen. Estrogen loss after menopause matters because the vaginal epithelium, endopelvic fascia, and levator ani contain estrogen receptors, and low estrogen reduces collagen content and tissue strength. Obesity, chronic cough, chronic constipation with straining, and repeated heavy lifting all raise intra-abdominal pressure again and again, pushing the organs against weakened support. Inherited connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan) and prior hysterectomy, which disrupts apical support, add risk.

Symptoms come from the bulge itself and from the organ involved. Women describe pelvic pressure, heaviness, or a sensation of something falling out, and may see or feel a bulge at the vaginal opening. Because gravity and abdominal pressure drive the descent, symptoms worsen with standing, straining, and at the end of the day, and they ease when lying down. Exposed vaginal mucosa can become dry, ulcerated, and bleed, particularly when estrogen is low.

blocks.title: Weighing the risk factors
blocks.text: A 62-year-old woman with three vaginal deliveries, a body mass index of 34 kg/m2, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease reports a bulge that is worse in the evening. Vaginal delivery was the initiating injury: it tore or denervated the levator ani and widened the hiatus. Menopause then reduced collagen strength in the fascia carrying the load, and obesity and chronic cough supply repeated rises in abdominal pressure that stretch it further. The evening worsening reflects hours upright. A nulliparous woman with the same weight and cough is at much lower risk, because her intact muscular floor still closes the hiatus and protects the fascia.

blocks.predict: Why might a woman with a large pelvic floor tear at delivery have no prolapse until her late fifties?
blocks.explain: The intact endopelvic fascia can carry the load for years; it stretches gradually, and menopause then weakens its collagen.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on load transfer from muscle to connective tissue.

blocks.text: The site of the support defect determines which organ herniates, and the organ determines the symptoms. The bladder and urethra lie in front of the vagina, so their prolapse bulges the anterior vaginal wall and causes urinary symptoms. The rectum lies behind the vagina, so its prolapse bulges the posterior wall and causes bowel symptoms. Along the anterior wall, the bladder sits higher and the urethra lower, so a cystocele bulges the upper anterior wall and a urethrocele bulges the distal anterior wall, just inside the vaginal opening.

blocks.title: Distinguishing anterior and posterior wall prolapse
rows: Distal anterior support and urethral attachments
Incomplete emptying, frequency, recurrent urinary tract infection
Pressing the bulge up helps the bladder empty
Leakage with cough, sneeze, or laughter
Pressing on the posterior wall or perineum helps evacuation
blocks.caption: Anterior wall prolapse gives urinary symptoms and posterior wall prolapse gives bowel symptoms.

blocks.text: In a cystocele the bladder base sags below the level of the bladder neck. Urine collects in this dependent pouch and is not expelled during voiding, so the post-void residual volume rises. Retained urine allows bacteria to multiply, which explains recurrent urinary tract infections, and frequency follows from the reduced functional capacity. A large cystocele can kink the urethra and obstruct outflow, causing retention and a weak stream; reducing the bulge by hand straightens the outlet and helps the bladder empty.

In a urethrocele the urethra has lost its support and moves downward when abdominal pressure rises. Normally the proximal urethra rests on a firm layer of anterior vaginal wall and fascia, so a cough presses the urethra closed against this support at the same moment it presses on the bladder. When that support is lost, the urethra descends instead of being compressed, bladder pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure, and urine leaks. This is stress urinary incontinence: small leaks with coughing, sneezing, laughing, or lifting, without urgency. It differs from urge incontinence, which results from involuntary detrusor contraction and is preceded by a sudden need to void.

blocks.title: Stress incontinence from a hypermobile urethra
steps: Unsupported urethra descends instead of being compressed
Bladder pressure exceeds urethral closure pressure
Small leak of urine without urgency
blocks.caption: Leakage reflects lost compression of the urethra, not an overactive bladder.

blocks.text: In a rectocele the rectovaginal septum is thin or torn, so the anterior rectal wall bulges into the posterior vagina. During straining, stool is pushed forward into this pocket rather than down through the anal canal. Women describe incomplete evacuation, the need to strain, and splinting, meaning pressure with fingers on the posterior vaginal wall or perineum to redirect stool. A high posterior bulge in a woman who has had a hysterectomy may be an enterocele instead, a herniation of the peritoneal cul-de-sac behind the vagina, usually containing small bowel, which reflects apical rather than mid-posterior failure.

blocks.title: Matching the symptom to the wall
blocks.text: Three women have anterior or posterior wall bulges. The first leaks small amounts of urine when she sneezes and has a bulge just inside the vaginal opening: a urethrocele. The second has recurrent cystitis, incomplete voiding, and a higher anterior bulge she pushes up to void: a cystocele. The third presses on the back wall of the vagina to finish a bowel movement: a rectocele.

blocks.predict: Why can a woman with a large cystocele have no leakage at first, then develop leakage with cough once the bulge is held up?
blocks.explain: The sagging bladder kinks the urethra, which obstructs outflow and masks stress incontinence; reducing the bulge removes the kink and reveals the lost urethral support.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on cystocele.

integration.text: Both topics in this chapter are anatomy problems before they are disease problems. The Bartholin cyst follows from a gland that secretes into a duct with a single small opening, and its abscess follows from infection in a closed space. Prolapse follows from a two-part support system in which the levator ani protects the connective tissue; once the muscle fails, the fascia stretches, and the position of each fascial defect predicts which organ herniates and whether urinary or bowel symptoms result. Physiology links each symptom to its cause: residual urine and infection in cystocele, lost pressure transmission and compression in urethral hypermobility, and trapped stool in rectocele.

The limits matter on examinations. Defects are often multiple, so one woman may have a cystourethrocele and a rectocele together. Stress incontinence can also come from intrinsic weakness of the urethral sphincter without hypermobility, and a large cystocele can hide stress incontinence. A vulvar mass that is not in the posterolateral vestibule, or that appears after menopause, should not be assumed to be a Bartholin cyst.

summary: The Bartholin (greater vestibular) glands lie posterolateral to the vaginal opening, drain into the vestibule, develop from the urogenital sinus, and are homologous to the bulbourethral glands.
A Bartholin duct cyst forms because the gland keeps secreting into a blocked duct; it is usually a unilateral, painless mass in the posterolateral vestibule of a reproductive-age woman.
Infection of the retained secretion produces a hot, tender, fluctuant abscess, usually polymicrobial and sometimes gonococcal or chlamydial.
A new Bartholin mass after menopause requires biopsy because the gland has atrophied and carcinoma must be excluded.

Pelvic organ support depends on the levator ani closing the urogenital hiatus and on the endopelvic fascia and ligaments suspending the organs; muscle failure transfers the load to connective tissue, which stretches.
Vaginal childbirth is the main risk factor for prolapse; aging, estrogen loss, obesity, chronic cough, chronic straining, connective tissue disorders, and hysterectomy add to it.
A cystocele bulges the upper anterior wall and causes incomplete emptying, frequency, and recurrent urinary tract infection.
A urethrocele bulges the distal anterior wall; the hypermobile urethra loses compression when abdominal pressure rises, causing stress urinary incontinence.
A rectocele bulges the posterior wall through a weak rectovaginal septum and causes difficult defecation relieved by splinting.
Anterior wall prolapse produces urinary symptoms, and posterior wall prolapse produces bowel symptoms.

verify: The clock positions of the Bartholin duct openings are given in different sources as about 4 and 8 o'clock or about 5 and 7 o'clock; this chapter uses 4 and 8 o'clock.
The age above which a new Bartholin mass should be biopsied is given as 40 years in many sources and as postmenopausal status in others; confirm what NABNE expects.
Typical Bartholin cyst size (1 to 3 cm) and duct length (about 2 cm) vary slightly between sources.
The relative frequency of Escherichia coli, anaerobes, and sexually transmitted organisms in Bartholin abscess varies between series.

The DeLancey three-level model and the pressure transmission and hammock explanations of stress incontinence are standard teaching models; confirm whether NABNE expects these names or only the descriptive mechanisms.

Whether NABNE uses the older terms cystocele, urethrocele, and rectocele or the current terms anterior and posterior vaginal wall prolapse, and whether it expects a grading system (POP-Q or Baden-Walker), should be confirmed.
